newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan president voices doubt on Hong Kong future.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan president voices doubt on Hong Kong future.

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui hailed on Tuesday Hong Kong's looming return to China but cast doubt about the territory's chances of flourishing under Chinese communist sovereignty.
"From the Chinese point of view, Hong Kong's transfer to mainland China is a delightful thing," said Lee, whose exiled Republic of China regards Hong Kong as part of China.

"But as for its transfer to the communist system, I am concerned whether Hong Kong can maintain a high degree of growth in its future development. Its prospects are both suspicious and worrisome," Lee said.

Lee, quoted in a statement issued by his office, told a group of Salvadoran journalists that he expected no problems during the British colony's July 1 handover itself but warned that Hong Kong's subsequent development was crucial.
"What happens after the handover is much more important and worth paying attention to," Lee said according to a statement issued by his office. The statement did not elaborate.
Hong Kong's future is laden with portent for Taiwan.

Beijing, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, has said Hong Kong's return, and that of Portuguese-held Macau in 1999, would leave Taiwan as the only territory to be "reunified with the motherland".
Beijing has said its handling of Hong Kong's return should reassure Taiwan about its own return under a "one country, two systems" model being pioneered in Hong Kong.
Under the system agreed by Britain and China in 1984, Hong Kong can maintain its political and economic systems for 50 years after it reverts to Beijing at midnight on June 30.
Lee has flatly rejected the "one country, two systems" for Taiwan despite his government's official policy favouring eventual reunification with the mainland.

Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government, which has embraced multiparty democracy, maintains that reunification is impossible unless the Beijing's Communist Party drops its monopoly on power and allows political liberalisation.
A survey sponsored by Taiwan's top China policymaking body appeared to echo Lee's concern about Hong Kong's future.
The majority of Taiwan executives interviewed by the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council said they were not optimistic about Hong Kong's overall economic environment after July 1.
Some 65 percent said Beijing would exploit its rule in Hong Kong to pressure Taiwan to make more concessions such as ending a ban on direct transport links between Taiwan and China.
More than 30 percent of Taiwan executives fear China may restrict their Hong Kong operations and treat them unfairly.

Hong Kong is an important transit point for more than $30 billion in investment that has poured into China from Taiwan since the easing of unofficial ties between Beijing and Taipei in the late 1980s.

Taiwan and Hong Kong reached an interim deal on Saturday that will ensure bilateral shipping links continue after July 1, allowing ships to lower their national flags when entering each other's harbour.
Beijing would not allow Taiwan ships to enter Hong Kong flying the flag of Taiwan's Republic of China, which the communists defeated on the mainland in 1949.
Taiwan has said it would permit Hong Kong ships flying Beijing's red five-star -- but only if Taiwan ships received a reciprocal welcome in Hong Kong.
Taiwan still bans all direct contacts with China.
